author: petrikrohn_26497
message: ## Why is the booter needed? The Falcon has a security coprocessor that can handle AES and RSA-3072. It can decrypt and validate its own code. The GSP process runs on the newer RISC-V core, which does not have the crypto functionality.  The GSP handles among other things the SMI interface. The encrypted GSP firmware is distributed as part of the driver package. The firmware is specific to each driver version.  As the RISC-V code cannot validate itself, the validation has to be handled by the SEC2 Falcon core. This validator is called the booter. The booter is not part of the VBIOS, but it too is loaded from the driver. (The host can load and launch any code on the Falcon in non-secure NS mode. To run in HS mode, the Falcon *u*code must be encrypted and signed by Nvidia.)  Note, that there are four (or six) different files at play here: The driver package contains the Falcon and RISC-V binaries in both production and test/debug format. The debug branch is not really encrypted, it is just obfuscated by a simple non-secret AES-key.  I do not remember the names of the files. I think `gsp_tu10x.bin` is actually the GSP firmware for Turing GPUs. The GA100 is Ampere, but the *booter* Falcon code is actually Turing generation, is uses the same booter code as older RTX 2000 series cards.  Of the Turing tu10x booters, you need to find the gebug version. Only it can be decrypted. Once you have the disassembled booter, you can create a gadget toolbox. With the gadgets, you can create a ROP chain. Start with a ROP chain for overwriting address `0x009A0204` with the value `0x02779000` to get 64GB working.

author: petrikrohn_26497
message: The driver loads three things to the GPU. It first loads the booter binary to the SEC2 Falcon and starts it in HS mode. It will then provide a signature file, which in our case is replaced by an oversized exploit with the ROP chain as the payload. The booter on the Falcon does not check the size of the signature. It accepts everything and overwrites its stack and return addresses. (It also overwrites the canary global which should prevent buffer overflows like this.)  In a normal case, the booter would then read the RISC-V GSP code from the host filesystem.  To make the exploit work, one needs a small modification to the driver. It must not check the size of the signature but must pass on the oversized signature payload.

author: petrikrohn_26497
message: ## arabella's results explained I will be commenting from memory, based on what I said on the original server and based on what was said publicly in Jon's paper.  The failure of the driver when more than 16k is written is explained in Jon's paper. This is where the canary global is stored in DMEM. It is a random value, so we do not know what it should be. Every function tests its local copy in its stack frame again the global canary. If they differ, the function does not return. Instead, it calls or jumps to a `panic()` function that puts the Falcon in a constant self-loop state. (The Falcon being in this state can be identified by a certain number returned somewhere.)  The Falcon has a 16-bit DMEM address space and a separate 16-bit IMEM address space for instructions. You can write almost 64k of data before reaching the end of the stack. We do not need an emulator like Jon had to create a ROP chain. The only relevant thing we need to know is the stack pointer of the `DMA()` function when it overwrites the stack. This frame on the stack is where we need to write the fake return address to our first gadget. From memory, I think the top of our ROP stack should be around 0xFF50. (I commented about the stack size on the old server. The size limits how many gadgets can fit into the size and how much liberation work can be done at once.)  If you remember, I commented on the disassembled 515 booter on the old server.  I noticed that there is strange line of code that jumps to itself. I falsely called it an "error handler". This is the `panic()` address. In the 580 booter, it is located at address `0x04A7`. The line in disassembly looks something like this: - `000004A7: 3e A7 04 00         B lbra 0x04A7`  In Jon's reference implementation, the value `0x000004A7` is also used as the fill value for all of the fake signature except the ROP. (See paper.) I cannot explain why, or if it is actually needed. Maybe this is the trick that lets us past the 36k barrier.

message: oh, what the AI suggested didn't quite work. Here's some slop it passed over to excuse why it didn't work:  "Good critique to engage with — but I think it's a misread of 0x10aa, and   separately, yes, I'd now recommend the emulator. Let me take both.    On the 0x10b9 entry (it does work)    The community member is reading 0x8224 as "BAR0Write(r10, r11)" and correctly   noticing r10 is pinned to 0x1c100 / 0x1c200. But those two addresses are the    BAR0-master interface, not the final target:   - I[0x1c100] = the master's ADDRESS register → gets r0 (our target PRI   address)   - I[0x1c200] = the master's DATA register → gets r1 (our value)   - I[0x1c000] = 0x800000f2 = the trigger → performs the external write of r1 to   address r0    So 0x8224 is just the low-level local register write, and 0x10aa uses it three   times to drive the master. Entering at 0x10b9 with r0=addr, r1=value   genuinely programs an arbitrary external PRI write — and the booter itself   uses exactly this path (0x29b8 → 0x10aa) to write its WPR2 registers, so r0/r1   provably survive the intermediate 0x1064/0x8264 calls. The approach is sound;   my failure was the stack offsets (the first-returning frame isn't 0x4d4, so   r0/r1 weren't where I put them), not the write gadget."

author: petrikrohn_26497
message: ## How to unlock? Why does Clanker think there is some hidden PLM controlling `FBPA_CFG1_BROADCAST`    at `0x009A0204`? I may be the reason. I oversimplified a bit on my Github post on the memory unlock. I did not want to tell too much of other people's work. Here is what is actually needed.  There are five values in the BAR0 address space that need to be changed for memory and compute unlock. Three of these need to be changed from SEC2 in HS mode. The other two can be changed from the host once the PLM unlocks them.  Change from SEC2 Falcon in HS mode - `FBPA_CFG1_BROADCAST`    at `0x009A0204`    set to `0x02779000` - `FUSE_SS_PLM` at    `0x008200FC` set to `0xFFFFFFFF` - `FEAT_OVR_PLM` at `0x00823804 `set to `0x000000ff`  Two other values can be changed from the host, after the PLM is set. - `FEAT_OVR_SM_SPD` at `0x0082381c` set to `0x88888888` - `FEAT_OVR_SM_SPD_1` at `0x00823820` set to `0x00000008`  The above information needs to be verified.

author: bigptoughneigh
message: The 0x1180f8 agent came back with a fully-verified answer:  0x1180f8 = NV_PGC6_BSI_SECURE_SCRATCH_14  Confirmed in the driver headers (dev_gc6_island.h:35, identical on tu102 and ga102): #define NV_PGC6_BSI_SECURE_SCRATCH_14 0x001180f8.  Why it’s not in the Falcon 16-bit space: it’s a host BAR0 register in the PGC6 “GC6 island” — the always-on (AON) power controller that stays powered during GC6 sleep. Inside it is the BSI (Boot/Security Interface) SECURE_SCRATCH bank: priv-masked scratch registers in the AON domain that survive engine resets and FLR. They’re the shared blackboard BootROM → FWSEC/booter → GSP-RM → Kernel-RM use to hand off boot state across resets. The Falcon’s own registers live in its 16-bit CSB/IO window (0x0000–0xFFFF); 0x1180f8 is the host register file at ~0x118000+.

author: bigptoughneigh
message: How the booter writes it — over its BAR0-master (external priv) bus as a read-modify-write, at the finalize step (0x1c0e):

author: bigptoughneigh
message: 1c35: r10=0x1180f8 ; lcall 0x1196   ← BAR0-master READ 1c3d: r10 &= 0x0fffffff              ← clear [31:28] 1c45: r11 = r0 << 0x1c               ← FFEC-derived nibble into [31:28] 1c4b: r10=0x1180f8 ; lcall 0x10aa    ← BAR0-master WRITE

author: bigptoughneigh
message: That’s the same gadget family the exploit hijacks — and it’s a different address space from the “0x1000 mailbox” (report_status at 0x1d0f writes falcon IO 0x1000 = the falcon’s own MAILBOX0, host-aliased at 0x840040).  The value semantics tie it all together:      •    0x11000000 = [31:28]=1 (finalize nibble) | bit24 (set by authenticate 0xccb). That’s exactly why our FFEC=0xDEADBEEF produced 0xf1000000 — its nibble 0xF landed in [31:28]. ✔     •    The named bit is bit 26 = BOOT_STAGE_3_HANDOFF (DONE=1) — the flag Kernel-RM polls (_kgspIsReloadCompleted, kernel_gsp_tu102.c:319) to know the SEC2-driven reload finished. 0x11000000 does not have bit 26 set — consistent with our rejoin landing the boot but not completing the reload handoff.     •    And it’s the source of our 0x29 horn: check_1180f8_nibbles (0x1c75) errors 0x29 unless [31:28]==0 && [23:20]==0.  So “finalize” is literally the booter stamping its boot-stage progress into this AON secure-scratch register that Kernel-RM later reads back across the reset boundary.
